reason: Attack failed, including the attack I thought would land. I expected eighteenth-century typography to capitalise the noun 'Slaves' but not the adjective 'Free', which would have made the card's 'born Free' a modernisation. It does not: both the Project Gutenberg 61143 text and the Duke scan of the 1730 fourth edition read 'If all Men are born Free, how is it that all Women are born Slaves?' with capital F and capital S, the phrase 'all Men are born Free' in italics. The card drops the italics, which is house practice, and changes nothing else. Locator confirmed in the scan itself: the running head two lines above the passage is '150 APPENDIX.' and the following page opens 'APPENDIX. 151', so the sentence sits on p. 150 of the Appendix. The Appendix identification is confirmed by the volume's own front matter: 'The PREFACE in the last Edition being extended to an uncommon Length, is now printed at the latter End, as an APPENDIX.' The preface of the last edition is that of the third, 1706, so the source line's '1706 Preface, printed as the Appendix in the fourth edition, 1730' is right. Cut is clean: the original continues 'As they must be, if the being subjected to the inconstant, uncertain, unknown, arbitrary Will of Men, be the perfect Condition of Slavery?', so the card stops at a genuine question mark and mints nothing. shipped.js: not shipped, no near match, Astell at 0 of 3, not banned. In scope (philosophy, 1706), publishable, tag Philosophy right. Source line leads with the name, no dash, 122 characters. Two softenings, not refutations: the evidence says 'the sentence closing that page', which overstates it, since the sentence's answering clause runs on to p. 151 and other text follows on p. 150, so the note should say the question mark falls on p. 150; and on the month's theme this is a challenge rather than counsel, which makes it the weakest theme fit of the four without putting it out of the month of aphorisms.
